newsitem.title: USA: State tobacco negotiators hit back at critics.
newsitem.headline: State tobacco negotiators hit back at critics.

text.p: State negotiators hit back Monday at critics of their landmark $368.5 billion settlement with the tobacco industry and warned that the agreement could break down if Congress made major changes.
Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, who led the arduous negotiations with the tobacco industry, said the agreement reached on Friday was not perfect but was a great step forward.
"To the naysayers I say: 'OK, guys, you do it. This country's been waiting 50 years for you to do it,'" Moore told a press conference at a meeting of the National Association of Attorneys General.
"Now, we've made a tremendous step forward here. The only people who will lose, if this bill is not passed, are the children of this country and the public health of this country."

The agreement has come under fire from some members of Congress and tobacco critics, such as former Food and Drug Administration Commissioner David Kessler, who say it is not tough enough on the cigarette companies.

The settlement, which would force the tobacco industry to sharply curtail advertising and marketing of cigarettes and to admit the dangers of using tobacco, is being reviewed by Congress and the Clinton administration.
Moore underlined the dangers of not finalizing the agreement and debating the issue for several more years, saying 3,000 children start smoking every day.

"How many more million people have to die from this product before we start doing something about it? We have a plan that will save lives now. My message to Congress is: Let's start saving lives now. Let's end the debate," he said.
Moore said the agreement could break down if Congress made major changes.
If the agreement were weakened, the states would have the right to push ahead with their lawsuits against the industry to recover costs of treating smoking-related diseases, he said.
Likewise, he added, the industry could walk away from the deal if more onerous conditions were imposed.

Moore and other negotiators planned to brief their fellow attorneys general at a private meeting Monday afternoon at a lodge in the majestic surroundings of Grand Teton National Park, where they were holding their summer meeting.
Several attorneys general said they planned to discuss how the tobacco money would be divided among the states.
Washington state Attorney General Christine Gregoire, who was closely involved in the negotiations, said she welcomed criticism of the agreement and said Congress had a right to its say.

"But in the long haul, if there is a significant undermining of the fundamental principles we set out to accomplish, particularly the public health ones, then I'm going forward with my litigation," she said. She added that she believed her fellow attorneys general would take the same stance.
"It's so comprehensive and so much of an advance over anything we've done over the last 40 years, that I think it would just be a terrible tragedy if we let it get by us," she said in an interview.
Gregoire was confident the states would agree on a way to divide the money. The states had mainly looked at a formula linked to each state's Medicaid populations, she said.
States that did not file suit against the industry would be treated the same as the 40 states that did, she said.
However, Moore said he would advise the other attorneys general not to come to a final agreement on dividing up the money because Congress would have a big say on the issue.
Moore said he planned to leave for Washington on Wednesday to brief members of Congress on the settlement. AMB.N
